newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk Islamist-led coalition faces crucial decision.
newsitem.headline: Turk Islamist-led coalition faces crucial decision.

text.p: Turkey's crumbling Islamist-led government faced a crucial decision on Wednesday with the expiry of the junior coalition partner's deadline for Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan to hand over power.

Erbakan, the NATO-member country's first Islamist leader, has so far ducked the issue of stepping down in favour of his pro-Western coalition partner Tansu Ciller in order to defuse a bitter row with the secularist establishment.
Ciller's True Path Party had set a June 18 deadline for Erbakan to resign and make way for a conservative caretaker to lead the country into fresh elections.
"Welfare is working with all its might for democracy and human rights. If sacrifices are necessary, it will make them willingly," Erbakan told his Islam-based Welfare Party deputies on Tuesday.
Welfare MPs gave Erbakan, whose voice quivered at several points, a standing ovation for the speech which had the air of a farewell salute to the Islamists' one year in power.

The powerful military's hostility to the Islamists has driven the unlikely coalition to breaking point and Ciller's party has threatened to pull out of the government if Erbakan failed to hand over power.
But Erbakan cannot hand Ciller his duties without first giving his resignation to President Suleyman Demirel, a veteran politician who would direct the formation of a new government.
Demirel's office said on Tuesday evening there was so far no meeting planned between the prime minister and the president.
Parliament must approve a power transfer and early polls but a string defections from Ciller's wing has cost the ruling alliance its majority in the 550-seat assembly.
A far-right powerbroker has said he would back government efforts to push the coalition's plans through parliament.
Support from rightist leader Muhsin Yazicioglu's eight MPs would give the government 282 deputies on paper, enough to win approval if they can hold on to their own restive MPs.
Military pressure has hindered Erbakan's goal of increasing the role of Islam in public life and building bridges to Turkey's Moslem neighbours.

The generals, who have staged three coups since 1960, say their fight with religious activism is a matter of "life or death" for Turkey, a secularist nation with ambitions of joining the European Union.

Erbakan presided at the weekend over the founding summit in Istanbul of the Developing-Eight (D-8) Moslem nations. But he has been helpless to stop growing military ties with Israel that have angered the Arabs.
Five Turkish navy vessels docked in an Israeli port on Monday in defiance of the prime minister's pro-Arab stance.
